Varazdin Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Varaždin, Croatia

Not demolished. Varaždin, first mentioned in 1181 and briefly Croatia's capital under Maria Theresa (1767-1776) before a devastating 1776 fire, later grew into a major industrial center. Jews arrived in the mid-18th century from Moravia, Hungary, and Austria; local authorities attempted expulsion five times without success. The community formally organized in 1807 (burial society from 1802), opening Croatia's first Jewish school in 1826 with 29 founding families. A magnificent Neo-Romanesque Great Synagogue, designed by V. Morandini and L. Deutsch, opened in 1861-62. Population reached 565 by 1921, working mostly in trade, business, and professions, with generally positive relations with other residents. Following German occupation in 1941, Croatian nationalists decimated the 515-member community (as of 1940), deporting most to their deaths; the damaged synagogue survived but was confiscated in 1951 and used as a cinema. This cemetery, established in 1806 and nationalized in 1958, holds about 600 tombstones with German, Hebrew, Croatian, and some Hungarian inscriptions; its 1927 Ceremonial Hall is a designated Monument of Culture.
